Hey Friv (and the other ~5 folks who read this thread)! I’ve got a question for you.

I suppose this question doesn’t really have to do with environments, but I figured it nonetheless makes more sense to ask it here than to briefly Zhu Long the previous thread.

Many “real” comic book characters often have one or more epithets.* Many of these are impressive titles, like The Man of Steel, The Man of Tomorrow, The Last Son of Krypton,** The Caped Crusader, The Boy Wonder, The Amazing Amazon, The Fastest Man Alive, The Emerald Gladiator, The Emerald Archer, The Manhunter from Mars, etc. Then there are also those that are more goofy nicknames, like The Big Blue Boy Scout, The Big Red Cheese, Shellhead, Winghead, etc.

So my question to you is, do you have any of these sorts of names for any of the Venture heroes? Is Wonderer called The Genial Genie? Is Greenheart The Leafy Champion? Et cetera.

And I suppose that this question does relate more to the nitty gritty writing of issues than the broader story arcs which have been your focus, so it does makes sense that it’s largely been unaddressed.

*I imagine the reason for this is that Golden and Solver Age comics typically had narration boxes accompanying every single panel, and reusing the hero’s name that much would be seen as poor taste.
**AKA 3/4 of the replacement Supermen.

posts.name: Chief Lackey Rich
posts.cooked:
Not me personally, although I’ve played at some table where some or all characters either had or grew into epithets - often involuntarily, like a nickname attaches itself to you. Villains tend to wind up with them in-play more often than PCs IME, in which case they’re usually at least mildly insulting and meant to mock the baddy.

The line between epithet and nickname seems hazy to me, now that I think about it. Mister Fantastic strikes me as a purely self-assigned epithet that most folks don’t use (to Reed’s quiet annoyance, no doubt), while Ben’s use of Stretcho could be either a nickname or a mildly sarcastic epithet.

The theory about epithets arising from caption boxes seems reasonable, but I note that they’re frequently used diegetically as well, with other characters addressing the owner with them as though the epithet was a name or title.

In the late 1960s, beginning with Edwin Sherman and continuing with new writer Matt Solares in 1698, a series of Covert Tactics stories began to wrestle lightly with the question of interventionism and how to best to handle the team’s fights against mad scientists and autocratic powers. Solares frequently used these stories to flesh out the competing drives of Kid Liberty, who favoured an aggressive approach, with the much more cautious attitudes of the Steward, who had centuries of experience in the potential for meddling in other societies to go wrong. Pulsejet tended to side with Kid Liberty, Irogane was more in line with the Steward, and Big Brain would shift back and forth depending on the situation, creating a complex team dynamic that was highly popular. New supervillains introduced in this period were driven by arrogance, greed, or beliefs in their own cultural superiority, forcing the team to protect innocent civilians from the machinations of powerful villains.

The Kurkani Civil War, however, took all of this to a new level. The storyline began in Covert Tactics #82, an issue that barely included the team at all, with the discovery that the small South Asian nation of Kurkan had been invaded and conquered almost overnight by an unlikely enemy – Jonah Drake, the Human Torpedo! The aquatic hero had taken it upon himself to organize a coup against the Kurkani Crown, seeking to dismantle the ‘malignant societal conditions’ that he saw as responsible for decades of violence by instilling strict moral and cultural regimens of his own devising. He believed that he could transform Kurkan into a gleaming utopia within two generations, and had just enough military support to undertake the effort.

Drake had had a run of antagonistic encounters with other heroes throughout the late 1960s. Raised under euthenicist principles, Drake firmly believed that with the proper upbringing and environment anyone could be physically, mentally, and morally upstanding, but he also believed that many of his fellow heroes lacked the moral and environmental training required to handle the problems that they faced. He was particularly harsh to heroes with criminal or difficult pasts such as Madame Liberty or Big Brain; while he applauded their drive to become better people, he believed that their pasts put a limit on how far they could improve and had clashed with several teams already over differing beliefs in how best to resolve dangerous situations.

But even for the Human Torpedo, overthrowing a country and trying to dismantle their culture was a massive escalation. Hoping that Drake’s old ally the Steward (one of the few heroes that he trusted and respected) might be able to talk sense into him, Covert Tactics deployed to Kurkan just in time to discover that the situation had already gotten immeasurably worse. Loyalists to the autocrat king, backed by a mixture of old guard believers and citizens who had been opposed to the crown but were now furious at having their way of life turned upside-down, had appointed Dr. Roach as the leader of their military efforts. With the Kurkani treasury at his disposal, Dr. Roach was using wildly dangerous experimental ionic technology to attack Drake’s military forces, as the would-be hero and the mercenary villain clashed across the country.
In Covert Tactics #83, the team was forced to fight a small fleet of Kurkani submarines enhanced by Roach’s ionic technology, who were planning to poison the coastal waterways to prevent the Human Torpedo from being able to join his forces. As Drake attacked the submarines on one side, Covert Tactics found themselves trying to fight the Kurkani navy and save them from drowning at the same time.

The Kurkani Civil War was a thinly-veiled critique of American involvement in the Vietnam War, but it just barely managed to squeak past the Comics Code by using the Human Torpedo as a rogue actor and not a representative of America. In the end, after a few issues of disasters, the team was able to convince Jonah that his efforts were doomed – he couldn’t force a country to become better, and his attempts to do so were just making things worse. Then, of course, they had to deal with Dr. Roach overthrowing his theoretical employers and declaring himself king of Kurkan. The storyline ended with the country in a cautious stalemate, with both the Human Torpedo and Dr. Roach removed from the equation and the loyalists and reformers entering into peace talks. It wouldn’t be the last time that there was trouble in Kurkan, or for that matter the last time that the Human Torpedo and Covert Tactics would interact as either allies and opponents, but for a time at least, peace was restored.

Behind The Scenes:

So Jonah Drake is kind of an asshole.

I wasn’t actually planning on including the Human Torpedo in my Silver Age stories! I thought it would be a while before he popped up again. But I wanted to do a civil war story that was a critique of Vietnam, but which wasn’t about US forces because that would never make it, which meant needing two villains with very different ideals. And I was looking at public domain art and got a picture of someone swimming at a submarine, and I thought, heck, why not.

And thus we get two Jonah Drake stories in this book! The Human Torpedo thought that he could completely rewrite a country’s culture to make it better, which is one of those ideas that should set off alarm bells and sure did for everyone who wasn’t Jonah Drake. This is definitely not the last time he does this, either, although he probably doesn’t screw it up this badly next time.

Dr. Roach is less complicated. He wanted power, he saw an in, he took it. Which is another reason to be careful of interventionism!

Skybreaker #150 featured an unusual sort of alliance between five of Skybreaker’s recurring foes, the most prominent of which was his nemesis Mary Molotov. Crime boss and alchemist Mr. Midas, who had parlayed his ability to temporarily turn objects and people into gold into a small but lavish gang, had set up a new gentleman’s club in downtown Grovedale and Mary Molotov was furious not to be invited. She easily infilitrated the club and laid down an ultimatum – she would prove she was the most feared criminal in Grovedale, and Midas would allow women into his club.

Amused at the idea, Mr. Midas went one step further. He invited three more of Skybreaker’s villains to take part in the challenge – the Lounge Lizard, a small-time lounge singer and part-time supervillain who could recover from almost any injury thanks to the curse he received looking to stay immortal, the Penny Pincher, a man who exclusively stole nearly valueless objects that would create vast amounts of chaos, and Prismatica, whose Rainbow Rowdies had been making waves in Grovedale’s criminal underworld. Mr. Midas issued a challenge to the four villains to put together the most successful and entertaining crimes, with the winner receiving a lifetime pass to his still-unnamed club.

Over the course of Skybreaker #150, the four supervillains launched a series of ever-increasing crimes, as Skybreaker was run ragged trying to deal with the fallout, racing to a new problem as soon as he’d dealt with the previous one and unable to pause long enough to actually catch his foes. As he did, Rhonda investigated the situation and discovered why so many crimes were being pulled at once, leading Skybreaker to attack the club directly to bring a halt to the proceedings. Mr. Midas and Mary Molotov were able to escape, but the other villains were captured, bringing an end to the proceedings.

Mr. Midas was so entertained by the challenge that he not only declared Mary the winner and opened his club to all genders, he gave lifetime memberships to all of the villains who had taken part. Moving his Crime Club underground, he set up a location where Grovedale’s supervillains could gather, brag about their criminal antics, and meet up for jobs and team-ups. The alchemical supervillain moved into more of a ‘fixer’ role, giving up personal schemes in favour of aiding and abetting the crimes he found so entertaining, and soon the Crime Club was a fixture in Grovedale’s criminal underworld.

The physical location of the club changed frequently, and it was raided by Skybreaker, Greenheart, and other heroes on a regular basis, but Mr. Midas was always prepared for heroic attack, with escape routes and traps laid out to make his patrons able to rest easy knowing that they could relax, take a load off, and not worry about getting arrested. Mary Molotov generously provided some of her demolitions expertise to help secure some of the clubs, although her enthusiasm did sometimes mean that a location had to be completely abandoned after the security system demolished the entire building. Still, it was a small price to pay for free explosives!

Behind The Scenes:

Okay, some pulling back the curtain here!

When I was first designing my next book, “Enemy Action”, the Crime Club was a supervillain team that I was in the process of developing. After a lot of back and forth, I ended up replacing them with the Dread Dynasty, but I had a bunch of notes already so I went ahead and fleshed them out as an environment here.

I don’t know if Mr. Midas, Lounge Lizard, or Penny Pincher will appear in future books. Mr. Midas probably won’t, he’s more or less fully-explained here. Lounge Lizard just got a mechanical writeup and there’s really not any more to him than what I listed I think, so he may be good. We might see Penny Pincher in a future volume, time will tell.

In her first two years as a superhero, Veilwalker had to contend with a number of plots by Elysium, Inc. to secure access to necromantic power. Elysium was hoping to industrialize the afterlife, using it for long-distance transportation, powering devices, and developing labour forces of spirits and ghostly beings. Their holy grail was to develop a reproducible method of ensuring that the dead would rise as ghosts, allowing them to sell immortality to the highest bidder.

As a rule, these experiments were carried out without any real care for who might get hurt in the process, turning innocent ghosts into agony-driven shades and giving random individual mystical powers that were very dangerous to their health and well-being. Elysium test subjects made up a third of Veilwalker’s opponents through 1969 and 1970, as she struggled to find a way to prove that they were responsible for the problems she was facing while also working to understand and develop her own powers, manage her personal life, and deal with the mystery of Asphodel and her own connection to the corporation and to Karita.

A Midnight Dreary was the two-part story that brought everything happening to Karita to a peak, and ended her first major story arc. As the story began, Veilwalker had been struggled over the past few issues with the mysterious Ravenmaster, a ghostly visitor who was stalking her for Elysium and trying to steal her magic away from her with his own tricks. His efforts were complicated both by the fact that he didn’t want to be doing it, being in thrall to Elysium, and the fact that Asphodel was secretly sabotaging his efforts in an attempt to protect her daughter from harm, but not so much that she couldn’t get useful data and power from him.

But Asophodel couldn’t stop the Ravenmaster forever, and in “A Midnight Dreary” he finally succeeded in laying a trap that neither he nor his mistress could sabotage. Veilwalker was lured to what she believed was an attempt by Elysium to capture a group of restless shades, but the site was actually intended to harness her own powers and steal her magic for the corporation to study. But Asphodel had thoroughly misunderstood how her daughter’s magic worked. She thought that Karita’s power came from within her, but she was just the conduit for it. The machines went haywire, connecting to necrotic essence so powerful that it took control of them and began to tear apart the veil between the living and the dead. As Asphodel scrambled to claim as much power as possible and the Ravenmaster spitefully egged the magic on to secure his freedom, Veilwalker was forced to try to contain the power, calming the spirits it was unleashing and sealing the rifts it was creating.

As the situation grew out of control, Asphodel was forced to choose between her research and her daughter. As a powerful rift threatened to pull Veilwalker back into the spirit realm forever, Asphodel used the accumulated energies of her gear to push Karita to freedom, dragging herself and the Ravenmaster into the depths of the afterlife. In her final moments, she revealed her true self to her daughter, and apologized for everything that she had done – and then she was gone, leaving Karita to struggle with the complexity of her mother’s latest cruelties and the sacrifice that she had made.

Asphodel would return, of course, as would the Ravenmaster, but her departure left Elysium in a shambles, and set the stage for Veilwalker to be able to focus more on the spirit world for the next few years. That story shift drew her into the Dread Depths crossover in the next year and set the stage for the formation of the Twilight Carnival.

Behind The Scenes:

For Dark Rivers, I wanted something that would touch on the storyline before Dread Depths kicks off and starts drawing Veilwalker more fully into the broader universe. I wasn’t sure whether to do something with her mother, or with the lost magical champions, but this came together nicely I think! We have the story of how she learned about Asphodel, a bit of complexity to their relationship for when Asphodel returns, and hints of a new villain who I may or may not develop further in the future.

Minor Twists

  • Ultraviolet Blood Cells: Half-Life’s radioactive immune system lashes out Roll the environment dice and create a number of d6 “Ultraviolet Blood Cell” minions equal to the Min die. Note how many cells were created. When a group of Blood Cells Attack all different targets, roll each minion’s die and use the highest result for each Attack.

Major Twist

YELLOW
Minor Twists

  • Fissioning Mitochondria: A nearby cell wall ruptures in a radioactive spray. Roll the environment dice and Attack one target with the Max die.
  • Internal Bleeding: You’ve found a danger area! Create the following challenge:
  • Fix the damage. Any bleeding still present at the end of the scene results in long-term injuries to Half-Life.

Major Twist

  • Red Blood Cells: A flow of oxygen and energy reinforces the immune system. Roll the environment dice and Boost and Defend one environment target with the Mid die.

RED
Minor Twists

  • Cancer Cells: Monstrous, voracious cancers attack everything in sight. Roll the environment dice and create a number of d8 “Cancer Cells” equal to the Max die. Note how many cells were created. Whenever a Cancer Cell destroys or incapacitates a target, step up its status die.
  • Sneeze: Half-Life sneezes. Roll the environment dice and Hinder all non-environments with the Max die. Attack them with the Min die.

Major Twist

  • Rapid Fission: Half-Life’s dimensional power tries to repair the damage being caused. For every two Ultraviolet Blood Cells that have been created, create one more. For every three Cancer Cells that have been created, create one more.

After a strong opening year, sales of Fallout began to go through a pattern of slipping and recovering. Introducing Isotope and building up the 238s as an ongoing threat kept sales strong through 1971 and much of 1972, but by early 1973 readers were drifting away again. In an effort to maintain the line and draw in new readers, the collection of writers and editors who were in the process of forming into the Political desk decided to help codify Half-Life into their world through a crossover with the highly popular Covert Tactics team. The two-parter took place in April 1973 and bucked the trend of many stories, giving Half-Life most of the pagecount of the initial Covert Tactics #133, and putting Covert Tactics front and centre in Fallout #30.

The lead-in to the story was simple enough – as Half-Life infiltrated a Neulyon lab belonging to the 238s, Covert Tactics was called in to deal with the radioactive outlaw, believing him to be the result of a super-science mishap who was a danger to himself and others. The team didn’t buy the story that Half-Life had created the nuclear explosion in Santa Juanita that changed his powers, but they did believe that he was unstable and potentially dangerous, and hoped that they could talk him down. Instead, they infiltrated a full-scale battle between Half-Life and Atomizer, a new member of the 238s with size-changing capabilities. Atomizer had lured Half-Life into a trap with the goal of infiltrating him and stealing the dimensional energies in his core, enabling the creation of new fissionable super-soldiers – and in the climax of Covert Tactics #133, he succeeded at the first stage of his goal, shrinking down and injecting himself into Half-Life’s veins! Half-Life’s body actually began to fission and grow unstable, threatening to detonate in the facility, which was still in the process of trying to lock him down.

Fortunately for the team, Big Brain was able to quickly analyze and activate Atomizer’s technology, using one of his robot drones. With Half-Life’s permission, the team entered the hero’s body to pursue Atomizer and stabilize the nuclear hero’s body. As Half-Life and Kid Liberty battled outside, the Steward, Pulsejet, Irogane, and Big Brain entered his body and began to do battle with his overcharged nuclear immune system, hunting down Atomizer and reversing the damage he was doing step by step.

The battle was hard-fought, with several pages delivered to the artist with the instructions to ‘draw something really wild here’. After most of an issue of struggling through Half-Life’s impossible anatomy, Covert Tactics was able to capture Atomizer, escaping through Half-Life’s mouth moments before Atomizer’s energies would have overloaded his body. With the 238s brought to justice, Covert Tactics agreed that Half-Life had ‘vanished in the confusion’, letting the undercover hero continue his quest but warning him that they might be sent after him again in the future.

While the issue was a fairly clear pastiche of Fantastic Voyage, and was largely an excuse to have Covert Tactics show off their capabilities in a particularly weird setting while Half-Life and Kid Liberty exchanged sardonic quips and fought gangsters, those were two things that comics readers were big fans of. The crossover was a huge success, and Half-Life’s grungier approach to the same sorts of problems Covert Tactics was dealing with brought a wave of new readers to Fallout, sustaining the comic and ensuring that Half-Life would become the more well-known version of Trevor Finn’s two heroic identities.

Behind The Scenes:

A lot of the ways that I design environments in the first stage is to look at the years I’m working with, see which titles haven’t had any issues recently, and then make something. I wanted a Fallout title for the Bronze Age, and I noticed that I’d made a quick note in my timeline about a Covert Tactics - Fallout crossover in 1973. Then I got “Quirky Event” and I was like, well, that won’t work, that crossover isn’t going to be quirky…

… or is it?

Because the idea of doing Fantastic Voyage but the body is radioactive and constantly splitting was hilarious to me. So here we are!

When Fly Boy began his battles against the Man, he quickly found that he needed somewhere to work on his suit, gather supplies, and stash gear that he’d recovered from the Company supervillains he was facing off against. In the first few issues of Fly Boy that place was his junkyard, but after a near miss with a wrist rocket launcher system in Fly Boy #5 he realized he needed somewhere that wasn’t directly connected to his civilian identity.

Fortunately, Tyrone’s friend and occasional flame Denise Fields was able to lend a hand. She’d found out his secret identity in Fly Boy #4, when he saved her from a gang of Company thugs trying to burn down her family’s restaurant, and was eager to help protect the neighbourhood. She also knew where all of the derelict and run-down garages, warehouses, and supply sheds in the area were, and who would be happy to take a bit of money to rent them out on the down-low without needing ID. With her help, Tyrone moved his gear to a burned-out auto shop and converted it into his Launch Pad, where he could stash the parts he was working on and the gear he saved for a special occasion.

It lasted fifteen issues before the Company burned it down.

Beth Horton, who had been lured back to Venture with promises of creative control after the end of Liberty’s Dream a couple of years earlier, had originally planned to have the Launch Pad be a proper secret lair that Fly Boy could use for his campaign. But Horton had been struck by the fact that Fly Boy was winning a lot of victories and it made the Man feel less like an overwhelming threat and more like a generic supervillain. She wanted Hank Ferris to be a dangerous nemesis, and the best way to do it was to give him some wins. So in Fly Boy #20, Ferris was able to analyse the superhero’s appearances, and track him back to his base of operations, and in Fly Boy #21 he sent some of his best operatives to take the place out and kill anyone who was present.

Tyrone was in the garage working with the Company attacked, and he quickly suited up to fight back. In the middle of the fighting, however, Denise arrived, hearing a commotion and determined to help. Fly Boy was too focused on the enemies he was fighting, and Denise took a stray bullet in the confusion and went down. Making a split-second decision, Fly Boy abandoned his base and flew Denise to a hospital whose staff he trusted not to spill her location, leaving his enemies to loot his gear and burn his lair to the ground.

The setback would lay the groundwork for a dynamic that would persist over the next several years. Tyrone would find a new location, set up his garage and gear, and start rebuilding, but it would only be a matter of time before corrupt police, Company goons, or Ferris Industries developers showed up and he had to clear out in a hurry. Traps and alarms could only go so far, especially since Tyrone was determined not to install anything that might accidentally hurt a neighbourhood kid poking around or a homeless person looking for a place to crash for the night. Instead, he kept his best pieces at home, and resigned himself to having to put his secret base back together each time that it became a little bit less secret, leaving himself more on the back foot than many of his fellow heroes and creating a sense that he was always struggling on the verge of being caught out for good – a dynamic that Horton successfully predicted would endear him to many readers and distinguish him from the competition.

Behind The Scenes:

I really like how this one turned out.

Giving Fly Boy a proper base of operations seemed like a great plan, but I wasn’t sure how to differentiate it from other hero bases. The randomizers gave me a ‘devastating unique twist’ for Red, and the most devastating unique twist I could think of was “whoops, everyone knows where your lair is”. But then that had to actually be something that was a threat in the story, or else why is it a twist?

Which led to “yeah, Fly Boy loses his HQ more often than you would expect from a superhero”, which fits the grungier DIY nature of his character really well and leads into some fun storyline bits.

The Weird West stories of Cryptic Trails created a network of strange locations and magical environments in the region around Lostwood, but with an unusual twist compared to many superhero comics. Instead of the hero being the one to explore a remote place and learn its secrets, Winter Wolf was already very familiar with all of the natural realms near his home. He knew how to protect them, and how to move peacefully through them. Explanation of these places was therefore usually given either in a monologue from the sasquatch hero to his foes, or when he was helping to protect humane or monstrous civilians who had wandered into a place where they were not safe.

Emmett’s Ridge was one of those places. According to Winter Wolf, there was a powerful spirit slumbering beneath the mountain, and her dreams caused life and land to mingle and drift, creating animals and plants with strange capabilities and unusual needs. Winter Wolf was not an ally of the mountain, but he knew how to slip past the mundane surface of the place and interact with its magic safely. In Cryptic Trails #33, a mining camp was set up on the mountain, and Winter Wolf knew that it was only a matter of time before the mountain’s spirit woke and its fury killed the hapless miners. But when he tried to warn them, they hired the Bickerton Agency to ‘clear out the monster in the woods’. Sensing an opportunity to test a new asset, younger brother Rudolph Bickerton used necromantic magic to summon the Boot Hill Monster, trusting that the undead gunslinger would be just the thing to defeat a sasquatch gunslinger once and for all. Winter Wolf found himself hunted along the crags of Emmet’s Ridge, as the mountain slowly woke to fury.

Winter Wolf was able to turn the mountain to his advantage, burying the Boot Hill Monster in an avalanche of molten snow that solidified into solid ice. The mining camp was abandoned safely in the chaos, with the hero escorting them secretly to protect them from the mountain’s wildlife and lull it back to sleep. The Bickertons would make a few more efforts to crush the magic of Emmett’s Ridge, steal what they could and kill the rest, but the mountain proved too powerful for them, and Winter Wolf was always able to contain the fallout.

Emmett’s Ridge would return in the 1990s in Twilight Carnival. In that grim tale, it transpired that the mountain’s spirit had been driven comatose by mining operations in the 1950s, and Emmett’s Ridge was no longer officially magical. As the mines dried up, the town of Emmett’s Ridge shrank back down in size, becoming a strange place with a stranger people touched by the slumbering nightmares of the mountain spirit. Most people never saw the mystical side of the mountain, but at the right times and with the right steps, hikers and tourists could find themselves wandering into the mountain’s reflection, trapped in the magic and unable to escape. The Twilight Carnival helped to calm the mountain spirit and begin restoration efforts, but the mountain remained a place that popped up from time to time for magical tales and weird mysteries.

Behind The Scenes:

For Cryptic Trails, I wanted a natural site that was more than a little unnatural, and a weird mountain where animals have plant or rock or wind mixed into them sounded like a fun time! It gets to be a proper Weird Locale in the past, and then turns into Definitely Not Twin Peaks in the 90s, before probably bouncing between the two over later comics. I may make use of it for a future story I have in mind, which I was deciding where to place…

As the Mystical desk grew increasingly strange, Madame Liberty and Reverie found themselves facing off against increasingly esoteric and unusual foes. Given free reign to write whatever stories interested her, Shannon Pace spent time playing with the nature of the world that her heroes were facing against, culminating in the creation of an entirely new branch of the fae courts that would prove deliberately short-lived, but whose manifestation echoed through the next couple decades of comics.

Courtless Meg had sought to regain her powers by stealing the courtly connections of other faeries, causing them to wither. She rampaged through the Underhill, and while Reverie and Madame Liberty were able to ultimately blunt her advance, many of her victims were cut off from the courtly magic that they had relied on to exist. In response, they began to gather together, looking for new sources of magic and ideology that they could transform into a courtly structure, and formed the Courts of the Forge. The Golden Court believed that the purpose of existence was hedonism, seeking pleasure above all else and tricking humans into bargains to serve them so that they would have to spend less time caring for themselves. The Glass Court believed that the purpose of existence was non-existence, deliberately seeking to fade away and leave no impact on the world. They did not end up becoming a major part of comics.

But the Iron Court believed that the purpose of the world was industry. They had been tricked by Courtless Meg because they had fallen for the lure of individual success, and the only solution was for every faerie of the Iron Court to cast their motivations and goals into the fire. When all were equal, none would suffer. When all were productive, none would be exalted.

The Iron Court abducted the Soviet hero Lockstep, trying to learn the ideology of equality from him and use it to their advantage. Excited at the opportunity to spread Communist doctrine to an entirely new species, Lockstep quickly found that the fae were far-too-able learners. They took his words literally, extinguishing their individuality and identities to become a nearly mindless, ever-ravenous, identity-destroying hive mind that spoke empty words of unity while tearing apart their countryside for resources.

As the Iron Court began to threaten the rest of the Underhill, Madame Liberty and Reverie found themselves up against a caricature of Communist ideology, a monster that even Lockstep recognized he had lost control of. There was no pride, no community, and no hope within the Court, only workers building weapons to conquer territories to seize workers to create weapons. He reluctantly joined forces with his old enemy to stand against the monster he had created.

At the end of the storyline, Reverie, Madame Liberty, Lockstep and Robin Goodfellow took on the mantles of the four seasons, unleashing them throughout the Iron Court and filling the gaps left in their natures. The effect of adding a second court structure broke the unity of the Iron Court, which returned its members motivations to it. The realm fractured into civil war, each faction trying to express their season’s nature through the Iron Court’s themes, and while the Iron Court would persist, it would become an increasingly fractured and internecine ideology as more courts were added to its structure. Lockstep returned to the Soviet Union, mourning the fall of a pure ideology into the infighting that he saw all too often.

Not a lot to say about this one, it’s mostly just a play on the Iron Curtain combined with fae weirdness. But I like the idea of angry Communist fae who are absolutely missing the point, especially in the late 1970s when you’re not going to get very friendly stories about them. It’s probably the first time that Lockstep works with the heroes instead of against them, and starts to lead into his shift once the Soviet Union falls.

In many ways, early Earthwatch served as a bridge between the Bronze and Iron Ages of Venture Comics, blending the social issues and general optimism of the prior age with the growing grittiness and darkness that would soon come to define comics in the mid-to-late 1980s. Earthwatch’s foes would also reflect this growing divide, mixing classical supervillains with political drama and questions about redemption and hope. Sometimes, this meant creating villainous political microcosms that also served as lighthearted japes, such as DOMIN-ION.

Built as part of an alliance between recurring Earthwatch foe Hive-Minder and the growing romantic duo of DOMIN-8 and Dr. Dufferin, DOMIN-ION was initially constructed as a mobile robotics factory able to secretly gather materials from scrapyards, industrial waste sites, and landfills and use Hive-Minder’s advanced technology to transform unwanted junk into devastating war machines. The new factory combined DOMIN-8’s Invictum chassis and designs with Hive-Minder’s ionic technology, and thus Dr. Dufferin cheekily dubbed it the “DOMIN-ION”, and the robots that it was building the “DOMIN-8Rs”, remote-service versions of DOMIN-8 that lacked her aggression and drive. Hive-Minder was deeply annoyed, but since he planned to steal the factory the moment it came into operation he let Dufferin call it whatever he wanted.

Of course, DOMIN-8 and Dufferin also planned to steal the factory the moment it came into operation. They thought Hive-Minder was looking down on them (they were right) and wanted to betray him and leave him in the mud. The instant the factory came online, both factions triggered their overrides, trying to steal control of DOMIN-ION and accidentally alerting Earthwatch to their location in the process.

As the heroes arrived to the facility’s first target, a massive junkyard in the eastern United States, Hive-Minder and DOMIN-8 tried to declare a truce long enough to deal with the interlopers. Unfortunately, each of them planned to use the other as a decoy, letting them wear themselves out against Earthwatch and activating the facility. They wound up leaving their factory largely undefended while Earthwatch rampaged through it, constantly butting heads and trying to trick each other into the line of fire. Caught between two masters, DOMIN-ION ultimately overloaded, self-destructing and leaving both Hive-Minder and DOMIN-8 to gather what they could from the wreckage and flee.

As a moral, it was a little bit on the nose. Either villain could have been happy with an army, but they wanted everything, and so they got nothing. The Steward even remarked that if the pair hadn’t been so focused on betraying each other, Earthwatch might never have even realized what they were up to until they were ready to strike. But as a gimmick, it was highly entertaining, and it led to plenty of good encounters between individual Earthwatch members and robotic foes, with the heroes working together and protecting each other in the exact ways that their enemies wouldn’t.

Of course, a mobile robotics facility was too good an idea to pass up. DOMIN-8 and Dr. Dufferin were ultimately able to reproduce DOMIN-ION several times, using the technology they’d stolen from Hive-Minder, and for his part Hive-Minder set up his own ‘Dominion Station’ on three occasions to fight the Celestial Travellers. None of the later factories survived for long; they were always discovered and destroyed. But they would become a core part of their creators’ stories.

Behind The Scenes:

I’ve been making a lot of factories lately, I should probably shift things up. But I do like the idea of Earthwatch, being formed to learn how to be heroes, getting front row seats to what happens when villains don’t work well together, and I like a factory just trying its best to make cool deadly robots.

Between this and SUB-MSF, I think it’s safe to say that Dr. Dufferin loves automated robot factories and also stupid puns.

World of Wonders launched into a complicated comics landscape, but it quickly carved out a place for itself as a breath of fresh air in the complicated landscape of Venture Comics. The Penitent had made a name for herself after her limited series the year before, and Lewis Maron was tasked with finding a set of magical heroes to join her and take on the role of globe-trotting heroes. He considered his recently-developed Hidden Corners characters, but was overruled, and fell back on some more well-regarded characters who hadn’t had as much ink spilled about their exploits recently – Wonderer, Dawn Rider, and Prometheus. The four heroes never had a proper team name, but they would end up helping to develop much of the magical setting of Venture Comics that would cover the next few decades.

One of the deliberately complicating factors of the comic was Susannah’s relationship to her family business. Van Horne Industries had been built on black magic and sacrifice, staffed with people chosen for their loyalty, greed, and ruthless dedication to profit, and safeguarded with all of the dark magic at Scion’s disposal. When she first inherited the company, the Penitent considered simply dissolving the lot of it and going it alone, but she quickly became convinced that doing so would only result in a half-dozen dangerous businesses sprouting up in its wake. Instead, she began the arduous task of rebuilding, while simultaneously dealing with her responsibilities as a champion of the magical world. She hoped that she could take advantage of her employees’ loyalty to redirect their attitudes towards more beneficial pursuits.

Within three issues, the first disaster arose. A vice-president of the company, angry about a recent directive to move away from selling dangerous industrial chemicals and redeveloping the company’s real estate arm to spend a portion of its profits rebuilding poorer neighborhoods, reached out to hire an assassin to take out what he believed to be a naïve and spoiled young woman with minimal understanding of her family’s power. He knew that Susannah had some magic, so he hired Avarice, and set things up to make it look like an attack on the building’s magic during a major board meeting that would ‘coincidentally’ end Susannah’s life.

Avarice arrived to discover that Van Horne Industries had far more magic than he’d expected. Delighted and empowered by the building’s hidden glyphs, he began a rampage that threatened to bring the entire headquarters down and kill dozens of people. Susannah ‘vanished’ in the confusion, using a collapsed roof to costume up as the Penitent, and sent out a call to the Wonderer to bring their allies to help.

As the battle raged, the increasingly-worried vice-president tried to reign Avarice in, only to discover that reigning Avarice in was essentially impossible. As he struggled to escape, a daemon summoned by the damage identified him as a Traitor To The Van Hornes and cut him down before the Penitent could save him.

Shocked by the incident, the Penitent nonetheless doubled down on her plans to reform her family’s business, firing several executives, hiring new employees from underprivileged communities, and even sending the minions of former enemies to get jobs in a company that might understand their unique needs. Many of the changes that she made were undone by the Scion of Silence during that event, leading her to have to repeat the situation throughout the 1990s, but over time she was able to shape Van Horne Industries from a cruel and vicious place to a moderately decent business empire with good benefits and open doors for victims of magical disasters.

As for Avarice, he ended up banished to the demonic realm that the Van Hornes had drawn their security from alongside the demons that the building summoned, caught in the backlash of the Penitent and Wonderer’s work as he drained demonic essence to survive. This time, no one expected him to be gone for long – even the Penitent agreed that the villain would likely find his way back to Earth soon enough. Avarice had, however, learned that there was a business out there with plenty of magic for him to snack on. Drawing on his own skills and connections, he spent much of the rest of World of Wonders finding ways to acquire, manipulate, or sabotage smaller subsidiaries of Van Horne Industries, using his unique abilities to drain their magical defenses and render businesses that had grown complacent from their good fortune vulnerable to hostile takeover. His ultimate goal was to take over the business, but the storyline was cut short by the Sovereign of Secrets event and when he resurfaced in the Iron Age, it was with only a few of his business interests intact.

Behind The Scenes:

One of my favorite retcons when I was working through my restructuring was giving Penitent the Principle of Business and making her the resident Rich Superhero. It fits her moral complexity and desire to do good with the profits of bad deeds, and it means that her company is as much an antagonist as it is a resource.

This helped write up one of the ways that could go, and since it needed to be a bit longer for pagecount it also gave a new story beat for Avarice, who previously only existed to appear in the Silver Age, never get mentioned again until he took out the entire Champions of Truth in a single storyline and kicked off a terrible revamp. Now we know what he’s up to in the eighties - being an evil businessman who will make deals with you and then steal your stuff. He’s not a good mercenary! Do not hire him!

The effects of the Sovereign of Secrets and their meddling in the timelines of the world weren’t limited to the heroes of Venture Comics. Through the mid-1980s, writers took advantage of the adjustments to revise, retcon, or otherwise alter the backstories and histories of several of Venture Comics’ villains. Mr. Ferris became a younger man, back in control of his Ferristown empire. White Mantis became two generations of supervillain, both drawing on the history of the original. Poison Pen’s stint as a small-time mercenary vanished along with much of her Silver Age history, moving her back into the shadows as a villain known to only a handful of heroes.

Not all of these changes were so direct, however. Because the situation with the Sovereign was a soft reset with an in-universe reason to exist, some writers chose to play with the situation, exploring how the adjusted world might affect characters more directly. Jordan Marks, taking over Champions of Truth, decided to have some fun by doing this with the Head Master.

In the “Head in the Clouds” two-parter in mid-1985, Marks revealed that Head Master’s predictive abilities were in absolute chaos. His powers were based on subconsciously gathering information from the past and present to predict likely outcomes with near-perfect accuracy, but the past was no longer a reliable source of information. A mess of stacked timelines had left the villain with crippling migraines and an inability to track what was happening or would happen, constantly reacting to situations that weren’t happening or preparing for eventualities that the Sovereign’s interference had wiped clean from existence. In a desperate attempt to repair his capabilities, Head Master reached out to a Dread Power. He opened a portal to the Empress of Ash, seeking to burn away the false timelines in his head and restore his power.

It didn’t take a master foreteller to know what would happen next. The Empress tried to seize control of the ritual, hoping to transform the villain into her latest minion for her assault on Earth. With limited understanding of magic and dimensional powers, Head Master found himself locked in a mental battle with a fundamental force of devastation as prophecy and fate began to burn around him. The new Champions of Truth arrived, but were quickly assaulted by both the forces of the Empress and the minions of Head Master trying to keep the heroes from their boss.

The resulting battle was fierce. Wonderer and Reverie repaired the damaged ley lines, Greenheart and Skybreaker took the battle to the streets and cleared away both the demons and gangsters that opposed them, and the Penitent sought out Head Master directly, severing the connection between him and his would-be rescuer and delivering a very impassioned speech about the absolutely insane danger that he’d put himself and everyone else in.

At which point the Head Master smirked, told the Penitent that actually, everything had gone according to plan, and triggered his contingency plan, escaping into a secret passage warded against magical intrusion and leaving the Champions to clean up his mess. He’d always known that they would respond to a sufficiently chaotic situation, and had deliberately planned for them to save him from a situation that he knew he couldn’t handle alone. The battle had cleared his powers, aligning him to the new timelines, and he was ready to become a menace once again.

“Head in the Clouds” served to re-establish the threat of the Head Master without undermining the Champions, while also helping to play with the complex situation of the post-Sovereign world and touching on the potential return of the other Dread Powers. It was a popular story, and would serve as a baseline for the increasingly complicated threats that the magical Champions of Truth would have to face.

Behind The Scenes:

A bit of behind-the-curtain into how some of these environments get made: first I line up the years and how many entries I’ve got, then I look at what comic titles are available in what years, then I see which ones line up with years in which I don’t know what’s going on in that comic, and finally I look for a villain I haven’t talked about recently and slot them in.

For 1985, I had a lot of choices, but most of them were titles where I’d already talked about what their first years looked like while creating the new heroes of the setting, and others were ones I was already committed to doing some extreme 90s for. Kicking off with Champions of Truth felt right, and I liked the idea that the first year of the new Champions mostly used their greatest hits - there are definitely also Doctor Freak and Congress of Deceit stories in there (even if the Congress no longer actually aligns one to one with the Champions). But an event that was “Head Master’s prophetic powers are all fucked up because time is all fucked up” was too good to pass up on.
